6.5 Organizing projects with folders
Now that we have a working multi-page app from the preceding recipe, in this recipe, we will
discuss some best practices for organizing our project. As our Streamlit projects grow, we need a
clean structure to keep everything manageable.

chunks.title: ainetworkingcookbook

chunks.content:
Chapter 6 179
Getting ready
Take a look at the preceding recipe and understand the concept behind main_app.py.
How to do it…
Create a project structure as follows:
network_management_app/
├── main.py # Main application entry point
├── requirements.txt # Python dependencies
├── README.md # Project documentation
├── .streamlit/
│ └── secrets.toml # API keys and secrets
├── pages/
│ ├── __init__.py # Makes pages a Python package
│ ├── dashboard.py # Dashboard page
│ └── config_form.py # Configuration form page
├── components/
│ ├── __init__.py
│ └── sidebar.py # Reusable sidebar components
├── utils/
│ ├── __init__.py
│ └── helpers.py # Helper functions
├── data/
│ └── network_metrics.csv # Sample data files
└── docs/
└── user_guide.md # Documentation
How it works…
Here are a few points about the structure:
• The main.py file provides a clear entry point for the application
• The requirements.txt file organizes all the modules required for packages and libraries
• The pages, components, and utils folders include a __init__.py file to make the folders
a Python package
• The structure promotes code reuse by organizing common libraries into folders
• The structure provides easy-to-follow documentation with README.md and the docs folder
Building an AI LLM Network Application Frontend with Streamlit 180
If we are to summarize the main concept, it is the separation of concerns. Each folder has its own
purpose and can be worked on separately. For example, documentation can be worked on by less
experienced engineers while the components can be worked on by specialists.
There’s more…
An additional folder can be added for testing to include unit tests, which are small, automated tests
for individual units of code or functions (https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html).
See also
The following document from Streamlit provides a great starting point for multi-page apps,
Streamlit architecture, and app design considerations: https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/
concepts.

In this chapter, we built a foundation for creating professional network applications with Stream-
lit. As a recap, we went from installation and setup to a “hello world” app, to learning the core
elements of Streamlit. As the application grew, we also learned how to organize our project, as
well as about deployment best practices.
One of Streamlit’s biggest strengths is that we can build sophisticated web applications using
just Python; no need for HTML, CSS, JavaScript, or web frameworks. Now that we understand
Streamlit’s fundamentals, we can start using it to connect AI LLM apps, add new components,
and start adding to the toolkit.
The network engineering field is evolving rapidly with AI and automation. New technologies

In the early days of the web, or even just a few years ago, we had one monolithic application for
our web services. We would use HTML/CSS/JavaScript for the part that the user sees, and we
would add some logic and code to handle the business logic and the connector between what the
user sees and the logic. Fast forward to today, where most web applications have now separated
the application into two main components: the frontend and the backend. The reasons for this
separation can be broadly categorized as so:
• Specialization: Developers can focus on user experience (frontend) or business logic and
data (backend)
• Scalability: When making updates, only part of the code base needs to be updated, thus
making it less likely to break and be more scalable
• Security: Most of the sensitive data lives in the backend, where it can be protected
One of the best analogies I have come across regarding frontends and backends is that of restau-
rants. The frontend is similar to the dining area and what the customer sees and interacts with,
whereas the backend is like the kitchen, where much of the work happens out of sight of the
customer: the customer’s meal is cooked and delivered to the dining area before it reaches them.
Each of these areas requires different skillsets and technologies, but they work together to deliver
the finished product (I don’t know about you, but now I am kind of hungry).

In the previous chapter, we learned about a simple way to create a frontend with Streamlit. How-
ever, much of the business logic still lives in the same Streamlit app we created. What if we want
to start using databases to persist our data? What about scaling our application into smaller
parts? We saw how we can just make API calls to OpenAI, but how about recreating a service just
like that for our own services?

service our application. We will build a FastAPI application that uses OpenAI’s GPT models to
answer network questions intelligently.

Let’s create a basic FastAPI application that uses OpenAI’s GPT model to answer network questions.

variable"
}

Here are the new SQLAlchemy key objects we need to take note of:
• engine: This connects to a SQLite database file called questions.db
• Base: We declare the Base class for database models
• session: This is a factory for creating database sessions
The database model includes the following aspects:
• id: This is used to auto-increment the primary key; it is an integer
• question: This is the user’s question; it is a string object

Building a Network Co-Pilot
When I started in the field as a junior network engineer, I had lots of questions, and I mean lots
of questions! Many of the answers could be found in books and online resources, but it took so
long to search through different sources and piece together the answer. Other times, the answer
took the form of tribal knowledge, meaning I had to spend hours looking through the current
configuration and ask more senior engineers, and then – maybe – get a decent answer. In short,
I wish I’d had a network co-pilot who could help me filter out answers, understand the network,
answer my questions at all hours, and just be my network best friend.
Well, this chapter focuses on building such a pal. Think of a network co-pilot as your AI assistant
that understands networking with the network data you are willing to supply. Instead of reading
through countless documentation and CLI commands, you can have a conversation with your
co-pilot: “Help me configure OSPF on this Cisco router,” or “Why does the interface error counter
keep on incrementing at midnight, every other Wednesday?”
A good network co-pilot does not replace a network engineer’s expertise; it amplifies it. It helps
us work faster, catches mistakes, and makes suggestions to help us get more done.
In this chapter, we will build the core components that make a network co-pilot work. We are
not building a full production app (because that would take another book to do so!), but we will
create the essential pieces that show you how it all fits together.
Here are the recipes we will cover in this chapter:

8.1 Model selection and evaluation
As we have seen in the book, choosing the right AI model is similar to picking the right tool for
a job. We would not use a hammer to screw a nail, and we would not use a model optimized for
image generation for our network engineering tasks. For this recipe, we will use three scripts to
evaluate different models:
• We will use a 1_test_models.py script to supply a few test questions and run them against
various models, in this case, gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4o-mini, and gpt-4o. We will save the
results to a file named model_test_results.json.
• In the second script, we will read the results and use OpenAI’s GPT-4o model to evaluate
the responses. We will save the evaluation to a file named response_evaluation.json.
• In the third script, we will read the evaluation file and average the scores across different
answers. We will use the cost of the model to arrive at a final recommendation for which
model to use.
Ready? Let’s see how it all works.

enable
configure terminal

```bash
router ospf 1

Assuming R1 has interfaces connected to R2 and SW1, you will need to

network 192.168.2.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 # R2's subnet
network 192.168.3.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 # SW1's subnet
```

Network monitoring has evolved over the years from simple MRTG (or RRDtool, as some prefer)
with SNMP to sophisticated observability platforms, ranging from vendor-based products to open
source projects. We can also collect network data from streaming sources such as NetFlow, gRPC,
or QUIC. In the early days, when it came to monitoring, the network engineer’s job might have
been to collect data from network devices. In today’s world, the network engineer’s job revolves
around making sense of massive amounts of data to take the right action.
In this chapter, we will introduce some practical approaches to AI-powered network monitoring
data, leverage the methods we used in other recipes (prompt engineering, chat completion, and
more), and implement the new Model Context Protocol (MCP).
Why MCP for network monitoring? For one, MCP is one of the most exciting developments in
the world of AI, and we should learn about it. Additionally, MCP excels in two areas that fit well
with network monitoring and performance:
• MCP excels at integrating diverse data sources and systems, and monitoring typically
needs to pull data from multiple tools, databases, and APIs
• MCP enables seamless context sharing between monitoring systems, ticketing platforms,
and performance databases
Network Monitoring and Performance Use Cases with MCP 246
In this chapter, we will cover the following recipes:
• AI-powered network health analysis
• Predictive network performance analysis
• Intelligent network optimization and auto-remediation
MCP is a relatively new approach, so a detailed dive into the technology is not possible within
the confines of a single chapter. We will begin our learning journey with an overview of the MCP
protocol and its key features.
For the recipes in this chapter, we will take a gradual approach to introducing different aspects of
the MCP protocol, ranging from basic to more advanced, via code. To help with our learning, we

MCP overview
MCP is an open standard that enables AI assistants to connect to external data sources and tools.
Typically, we would build each integration like so:
AI Assistant -> Different Integrations [A-Z] -> Network Tool [A-Z]
However, MCP allows a uniform connector to be used so that an AI assistant can talk to it:
AI Assistant -> MCP Protocol -> Network MCP Server -> Network Tools [A-Z]
MCP concepts
There are a few concepts we should know about before we get started:
• MCP URIs: MCP URIs are logical identifiers that specify which information or capabilities
you want to access. The structure is scheme://path, which is different from the REST API
format we are familiar with. They are logical identifiers.
• MCP resources: Resources are read-only data sources that provide information. The main
point is that these have read-only data.
• MCP tools: Tools are executable functions that can perform actions or operations. These
are actions AI can invoke to do things.
• Context and state: MCP servers are designed to be stateless; each request is independent
of previous interactions.
• Error handling and input validation: Network tools must validate inputs and handle
errors correctly due to their impact.
